html:
From 1864 to 1897 France sent convicts to New Caledonia, mostly to Île Nou in the harbour of Nouméa. Many stayed after their sentences as small farmers.

After the Paris Commune of 1871, thousands of Communards were deported here, among them the teacher Louise Michel, who befriended Kanak and supported their revolt. Algerian rebels from the Kabylie uprising of the same year were sent too, and their descendants still live on the island.

Freed convicts and settlers took up land seized from the Kanak, sharpening the clash that broke out in the revolt of 1878. Their descendants, the Caldoches, form much of the population opposed to independence today. Compare convict transportation to Australia.
